newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Third World says cannot protect environment.
newsitem.headline: Third World says cannot protect environment.

text.p: Third World nations told the U.N. Earth Summit this week that they cannot protect the environment because of deep cuts in foreign aid and broken pledges by rich countries.

From Mongolia to Zimbabwe, speakers said they had severe problems in wiping out poverty and that private investment was concentrated in too few countries, foreign aid had fallen and debt-relief was nowhere in sight.
Several said that in the struggle to provide meagre basic services, attention had to be be diverted from "sustainable development" --- environmentally-friendly economic growth.

"If financial resources were forthcoming, Africa would refrain from killing wild animals for food, cutting down trees for fuel or polluting water resources for lack of appropriate technologies," said Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe.
"The World Trade Organisation has assisted transnational corporations with global economic opportunities but has not inculcated responsibilities of the environment," he said

The Earth Summit, which ends on Friday with a document that will be high on promises but low on commitments, is reviewing progress since a landmark environmental summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago.

But since Rio, forests, farmlands and coral reefs have dwindled, pollution is increasing, oceans are overfished and 1.3 billion people are so poor they threaten to use any resource available just to stay alive.

"Due to lack of financial resources, many poor developing countries are compelled either to reallocate their already stretched budgets in order to implement recommendations of the Earth Summit or to defer their implementation," said Mongolian Environment Minister Aduasuren Tsohio.
British Environment Minister Clare Short told a panel that so-called "globalization" could both create more economic wealth and "marginalize more people."
"We need more institutions to control globalization, to make it meet the needs of humanity." she said.
According to World Bank reports, foreign investment flows to only 12 developing countries with only one percent in sub-Saharan Africa.

Consequently some countries would like government foreign aid targeted to improvements in their infrastructure to attract private capital while others stress that trade policies have to be further liberalised so their commodities and raw materials can find an outlet.
Uganda's Foreign Minister Martin Aliker said on Thursday there must be an "enabling international environment conducive to economic growth and development"
"For Uganda this is particularly urgent in the areas of increased investment and export trade and enhanced debt-relief," he said.
Over the last five years, industrial countries, especially the United States, have been preoccupied with balancing their budgets and have slashed foreign aid.
Official government aid has declined to an average of 0.27 of gross domestic product among industrial states compared to 0.33 percent in 1992, with the biggest cut registered in the United States.
And the so-called peace divided at the end of the Cold war has failed to materialise.

"The end of the Cold War was more effective in eliminating Great Power rivalry as a motivation for aid than it was in bringing about widespread disarmament," the Washington-based Worldwatch Institute concluded.
